title: The Over-Soul
hook: he wrote of a great soul in which each person's life is contained (The Over-Soul)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Emerson's Compensation: every act rewards itself, and the dice of God are always loaded. Your line was it comes back. What did one choice make of you? Day one thousand two hundred.

A spring comes up out of a hillside. Clear water, out of the dark, out of rock, from somewhere nobody can point to. Follow it downhill and it becomes a stream, then joins other streams, and somewhere far below it is a river. The water at the spring has no idea about the river. Near the start of one of his essays, Emerson turns that picture on us: "Man is a stream whose source is hidden." We don't know where our lives come from, he says. They descend into us from somewhere we can't see. The essay is called The Over-Soul, and it's about that hidden source.
screen: `A SPRING OUT OF THE ROCK.` → `A STREAM WHOSE SOURCE IS HIDDEN.` → `THE OVER-SOUL.`

segments.voice: First, the problem. Emerson says: "We live in succession, in division, in parts, in particles." That's ordinary life. One thing after another. Me over here, you over there. A day chopped into tasks. A self chopped into roles. Second, what he says is underneath. Within each person, Emerson writes, is the soul of the whole, the wise silence, the universal beauty to which every part is equally related. He gives it a name: the Over-Soul. And he describes it as a unity within which each person's particular life is contained, and made one with all the others. Not a soul floating somewhere above us. A larger life we're each already inside of. Third, how he says we notice it. Not by argument. Emerson says it shows up in moments: in a conversation where two people suddenly understand more than either brought to it, in a sudden insight, in the quiet behind thought. He calls it a common heart. In his picture, the little self, with its worries and its name, sits inside something much larger. Fourth, why this changes the week we've had. Trust thyself and insist on yourself could sound like a lonely road. The Over-Soul is the other half. The self Emerson trusts is a door into what everyone shares. That's why self-reliance, read carefully, opens out rather than closing in. Some readers hear echoes of older traditions here. Emerson's reading from India gets its own day later in this block.
screen: `IN PARTS, IN PARTICLES.` · `THE SOUL OF THE WHOLE.` · `A CONVERSATION, A COMMON HEART.` · `THE SELF IS A DOOR.` · then, large: `THE WISE SILENCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: feel part of something larger. Settle, and let the breath slow. Notice the edges you usually live inside: this body, this name, today's list. Then let your attention widen. The room around you. The people in the building or the street. The city, the weather moving over it. The breath you're taking now was outside you a moment ago, and will be outside you again. Let the edges soften a little. Rest as one stream in a much larger river. The bell holds the time.
The Over-Soul. Emerson's name for the larger life in which each person's life is contained and made one with all the others: the soul of the whole, the wise silence. Today's word.
Your line: contained in something larger. Once today, in a crowded place, look around and remember Emerson's picture: every person there a stream from a hidden source. Day one thousand two hundred.

howItsDone: Some readers of Emerson's The Over-Soul take it as an invitation to notice the larger life they share with others, in moments of insight, quiet, or real conversation.

notes: Confirm exact wording of the two quotations against the 1841 text. Note: 'Man is a stream whose source is hidden' is from the essay's second paragraph, after an opening paragraph on moments of faith and vice; the script says 'near the start'.

The phrases 'the soul of the whole; the wise silence; the universal beauty' and 'within which every man's particular being is contained and made one with all other' are given without quotation marks and cited as paraphrase; confirm wording if a reviewer wants them quoted.
'Some readers hear echoes of older traditions here' makes no specific claim; day 1208 (Brahma) treats his reading of the Upanishads and the Gita.
The spring-and-river hook is the narrator's illustration, built on Emerson's stream image.
